Yashita Aggarwal 6mo Edited Report this post I was using Myntra ’s Wishlist recently, trying to buy something I had saved weeks ago.
What should’ve been a quick decision turned into… scrolling. A lot of it. 🤔 

As I dug deeper during a feature analysis assignment, the reason became clear.

Here’s the story the Wishlist was telling 👇
🔍 Pain points I discovered:
• Out-of-stock items often appear before purchasable ones, hiding what users can actually buy
• There’s no clear visual distinction between available and unavailable items
• As wishlists grow, finding relevant items becomes effort-heavy instead of helpful

What started as a “save for later” feature slowly turns into decision fatigue.

💡 The insight:
Wishlist users aren’t browsing — they’re ready to act. And every extra scroll delays that action.

🛠 How this shapes my PM thinking:
Good product design isn’t about adding more features — it’s about removing friction at the moment of intent.

📊 Full breakdown with solutions in my deck below 👇

Avneesh Singh 1y Report this post A #UX Flaw in Myntra’s Wishlist: How Many In-Stock Items Are You Missing?

Wishlist functionality in e-commerce apps is crucial—it helps users track items they love and buy them later. But what if a UX gap makes users believe their desired products are out of stock when they’re actually available?  

While using Myntra’s Wishlist, I noticed something odd. At first glance, it showed around 15-20 in-stock items, followed by out-of-stock products. Naturally, one would assume that everything beyond this point is unavailable. However, when I scrolled further, a refresh occurred, and more in-stock items suddenly appeared -ones that were previously hidden behind the out-of-stock section.  

Why is this a problem?  
1. False Scarcity Perception– Users may assume items they saved are no longer available and leave the app without purchasing.  
2. Missed #Revenue Opportunity – A potential sale is lost simply because an in-stock item isn’t surfaced properly.  
3. Frustrating UX – Users who don’t scroll far enough might abandon their Wishlist altogether.  

The Fix?  
Instead of prioritizing out-of-stock items too early, #Myntra could:  
✅ Load all in-stock items first before showing out-of-stock ones.  
✅ Improve visibility by clearly indicating more items are available with a “Load More” button or seamless infinite scroll.  

A small UX tweak could lead to better conversions, improved user trust, and a smoother shopping experience.

G Lakshmi Narasimha 7mo Report this post It’s a great example of how small UX shifts can drive real business impact.
The idea of converting the Wishlist from a passive list into an active decision making space is powerful.
The Wardrobe structure reduces cognitive load, while Try Now bridges the gap between intent and action.
What I really like is how this concept aligns with existing Myntra UI patterns instead of reinventing the experience making it feel realistic and scalable.
Strong thinking around user behavior and conversion 👏 Harishwar Goud 7mo I built a product concept for Myntra focused on improving the Wishlist journey and accelerating purchase decisions.

The core idea is to transform the Wishlist from a passive storage space into a more structured, decision-friendly experience using a feature called Wardrobe where saved items are organized into categories and a Try Now feature where users can build outfits from items already in their Wishlist.

This concept is grounded in user behavior, decision fatigue, and real shopping patterns, with a focus on improving wishlist-to-cart conversion and Average Order Value.
